segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Hello and welcome to Real Easy English, the podcast where we have real conversations in easy English to help you learn.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: I'm Beth.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And I'm Neil. You can read along with this podcast and find a worksheet to help you learn on our website, bbclearningenglish.com.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Neil, how are you?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: I'm really well, Beth. How are you?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: I'm all right, thank you. Today we're talking about food shopping and we'll talk about the kinds of foods that we buy.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: OK, let's get started. So, Beth, how often do you go food shopping?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Oh, quite often. I think I go maybe two or three times a week.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: I prefer to get smaller shops because then you get fresher ingredients rather than doing one big food shop.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: and it also gets me out of the house.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: What about you?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: I would like to go shopping once a week,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: but there isn't enough room in my fridge

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: for all the food that I need for a week

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: and I'm not organised enough.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: So I go often every day, every other day maybe.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Okay so Neil what sorts of foods do you buy every week generally

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Well I buy staples things like pasta rice bread potatoes the basic parts of a meal that fill you up

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And I usually think about what meals we want to have and then get the ingredients for those.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Yeah, I'm the same. I would say we normally buy a bag of pasta and we normally have a loaf of bread once a week.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: But then if I buy something like cereal, we don't have that too often.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So I might get a box of cereal maybe once a month and that lasts us for the whole month.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: I get a jar of marmalade every week because I love marmalade so much and I'm the only person who eats it in my house.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: You must have so much marmalade on your toes to go through one a week.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: That's crazy.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: I love it.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: OK, so we've talked about bread.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: We both like a loaf of bread when we go shopping.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: But the grammar of that is quite interesting, isn't it?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: So when we have a noun like bread or rice or jam which is uncountable you can count it We need something to describe what it in So we have a loaf of bread and that makes it countable a loaf

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: A jar of honey or jam.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: A bag of pasta.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Yeah, exactly. We can't say pastas or breads or rices.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: It just sounds really weird. So you'd need to say,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: oh, please remember to buy a loaf of bread.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Or you could say, please buy some bread.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Yeah. Now, some nouns are countable and uncountable. For example, if you say, I'm going to buy some chicken and I'm going to buy a chicken, what's the difference?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So, if you buy some chicken, it means parts of chicken, like maybe chicken legs or chicken breasts. Whereas if you say a chicken, it means a whole chicken.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: A dead one.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Some food, though, is simpler, grammatically.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: So, for example, you can count an apple or a banana.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: So you can say apples, bananas, just a normal plural.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Exactly, yeah. I could buy an apple or I could buy five apples and that is very simple.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Whereas something like tuna, you can't buy tunas. It has to be a tin of tuna.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Beth, when you go shopping, do you make a list?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: No I kind of have a list in my head but then I go a bit crazy when I get there You should never go shopping when you hungry

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: That true

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: What about you

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: I always take a list and even when I have a list sometimes I forget things

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Oh dear.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And also, sometimes I can't read the words on the list that I've written.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Let's recap the vocabulary we heard during the conversation.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: We had shopping list all the food you need to buy written down so you remember it.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And we talked about lots of foods we buy which are uncountable nouns.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: So when we buy these, we have some useful ways to talk about them.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: For example, we buy a loaf of bread.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: A bag of pasta.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: A jar of honey or my favourite, marmalade.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And some chicken.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: But you can also buy a chicken that's a whole chicken.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: then it would be a countable noun, just like apples and bananas.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: That's it for this episode of Real Easy English.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: To test what you've learned, try the worksheet on our website.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Next week, we'll be talking about houses.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: See you then.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Bye.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Bye.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: you
